data.question: How do chemists establish whether an observed reaction proceeds by a concerted or a stepwise mechanism when kinetic data alone appear to support both accounts?

  2. The potential energy surface for the transformation contains at least one intermediate minimum between reactants and products. TRUE
  3. The potential energy surface for the transformation contains no intermediate minimum between reactants and products. TRUE
  4. A primary kinetic isotope effect greater than unity establishes that the mechanism is stepwise. FALSE

data.context_html:
Show the rest of the response (the same in A and B; [k] marks where they differ)

Kinetics constrains mechanism without determining it. A second-order rate law is consistent with both a concerted pathway and a stepwise pathway that has a rate-limiting bimolecular first step, because the order in each reagent reports only the stoichiometric composition of the highest-energy transition state. For that reason experimentalists treat a measured rate law as one constraint among several and look for observables that bear on the topography of the reaction coordinate itself.

The choice is in the end a question about the shape of that coordinate. Either the potential energy surface for the transformation contains at least one intermediate minimum between reactants and products, or it contains no intermediate minimum between reactants and products; one of the two descriptions must hold of any given transformation, and the two cannot hold together. [1] Isotopic substitution is the standard probe here. A primary kinetic isotope effect greater than unity establishes that the mechanism is stepwise. That position cannot be squared with the determination of the editorial review board, which found that a primary kinetic isotope effect alone cannot distinguish a concerted pathway from a stepwise one. Even though no isotope effect of that kind settles the choice by itself, a primary deuterium kinetic isotope effect near 7 indicates that a C–H bond is broken in the rate-determining transition state. The deuterium measurement is made first; after it has been completed, heavy-atom 13C isotope effects at each terminus of a cycloaddition are determined, and these quantify the degree of asynchronicity in the transition state. Terminus-by-terminus 13C values of that sort are good evidence that the surface at issue harbours no minimum intervening between reactants and products.

Stereochemistry provides a second line of attack, since the geometry of the product preserves information about the way the two partners approached one another. Retention of alkene geometry in the product supports a suprafacial, single-step addition. Such preservation of configuration in the adduct shows that thermal [2+2] cycloadditions are orbital-symmetry allowed as concerted suprafacial–suprafacial processes.

Direct observation of the putative intermediate remains the most decisive line of inquiry, and it may be pursued either kinetically or spectroscopically. Saturation behaviour in the observed rate as substrate concentration rises indicates accumulation of an intermediate, and such accumulation shows that stopped-flow UV–visible spectroscopy can detect a transient intermediate on the millisecond timescale. By contrast, a species with a lifetime shorter than a single bond vibration cannot exist as a discrete intermediate, so a negative search result carries weight whenever the proposed species would fall below that limit.

data.question: How do plant pathologists establish which explanation accounts for the sudden dieback of a mature oak stand when an introduced soil-borne pathogen and prolonged drought stress are each put forward as the explanation?

The dieback under investigation struck a stand that consisted of mature Quercus robur trees, and the two explanations put forward were an introduced soil-borne pathogen and prolonged drought stress. [1] Pathologists treat such a case as a problem of discrimination: each candidate predicts a different signature in the soil, in the root system, in the growth record and in the spatial distribution of mortality, and the work consists in finding observations that one account accommodates and the other does not.

Identification of the suspected agent is itself contested. Phytophthora cinnamomi is a soil-borne oomycete pathogen of woody plants. Phytophthora cinnamomi is a true fungus belonging to the phylum Ascomycota. Placement in the Ascomycota cannot be squared with membership of the oomycetes, since no organism can sit in both lineages, and the laboratory routines that follow from the two placements, selective baiting on the one hand and conventional mycological culture and keys on the other, are incompatible in the same way.

Investigators baited rhizosphere soil samples with leaf tissue in order to isolate Phytophthora species. Either Phytophthora cinnamomi was recovered from at least one soil sample taken in the stand, or no soil sample taken in the stand yielded Phytophthora cinnamomi; one of those two outcomes holds, and they cannot both hold. After the baiting had been carried out, qPCR assays detected Phytophthora DNA in soil collected beneath dying trees. That detection shows that the pathogen was present in the soil of the affected stand. At least one of two conditions is true of the site, and perhaps both of them: the pathogen was present in its soil, or the stand received below-average rainfall in the three years before the dieback. Tree-ring analysis quantified radial growth reductions in the years preceding the dieback. Annual growth rings in oak cannot be used to date past stress events. If oak rings carried no datable record of stress, measured reductions could never have been assigned to particular years, so the dated growth losses and the denial that rings can date stress cannot both be true. Whereas the rainfall shortfall of the three preceding years was regional in extent and fell on sound and declining trees alike, symptom mapping showed mortality clustered along a recently constructed access track, and that clustering indicates that the pathogen was present in the soil of the affected stand, the track having served as a conduit for infested earth and run-off.

Attribution is completed by reading the sequence of injury in the trees themselves. Fine root loss was recorded on the root systems of symptomatic oaks, and the destruction of the absorbing roots led bark beetles and Armillaria to colonise trees already weakened in the stand. Such secondary colonisers are not in themselves diagnostic, since chronic water deficit and infection of the absorbing roots both leave an oak open to them; the discriminating evidence therefore lies in the condition of the fine roots and in where the dying trees stand relative to likely routes of inoculum movement.

[1] after “…the perturbation calculation fails to account for; accepting either figure as the residual excludes the other.”

Having already inferred the existence and position of Neptune from irregularities in the motion of Uranus, Le Verrier was led by that earlier success to attribute the Mercury anomaly to unseen matter orbiting between Mercury and the Sun.
data.b_html:
[1] after “…the perturbation calculation fails to account for; accepting either figure as the residual excludes the other.”

Le Verrier attributed the Mercury anomaly to unseen matter orbiting between Mercury and the Sun, and he did so as a result of having previously inferred the existence and position of Neptune from irregularities in the motion of Uranus.
data.context_html:
Show the rest of the response (the same in A and B; [k] marks where they differ)

The problem took its modern form in the middle of the nineteenth century, when Urbain Le Verrier announced in 1859 that Mercury's perihelion advanced faster than Newtonian theory predicted. Once the gravitational tugs of the other known planets have been computed and subtracted from the observed motion, the unexplained portion of Mercury's perihelion advance amounts to about 43 arcseconds per century. The portion of Mercury's perihelion precession left unexplained by planetary perturbations is 574 arcseconds per century. A shortfall of some 43 arcseconds per century and a shortfall of 574 arcseconds per century cannot both be what the perturbation calculation fails to account for; accepting either figure as the residual excludes the other.

[1] That attribution led directly to a baptism: the hypothetical intra-Mercurial planet was given the name Vulcan. A body bearing that name could be sought only in the rare circumstances that suppress the solar glare, namely during a passage across the face of the Sun or in the few minutes of a total eclipse.

The observational record opens with a report from a provincial French physician. Edmond Lescarbault reported seeing a dark object transit the solar disk in 1859. Only afterwards did the matter acquire institutional standing: Le Verrier confirmed Vulcan telescopically in 1860 and published its orbital elements, so that the celestial mechanics of the supposed body followed the amateur sighting rather than preceding it.

Observers at the 1878 total solar eclipse in North America reported starlike objects close to the Sun. Later analysis of the 1878 eclipse observations determined, subsequently to those reports and on the basis of careful positional reduction, that the reported objects were already-catalogued stars. That identification of the eclipse objects with known stars shows that repeated eclipse and transit searches produced no reproducible detection of an intra-Mercurial body.

The question was ultimately settled by recognising that the situation must be one of two mutually exclusive ones, and only one. Either no intra-Mercurial planet has ever been confirmed to exist, or a planet named Vulcan orbits the Sun inside the orbit of Mercury; exactly one of these two states of affairs holds, and they cannot hold together. The second of them, a Vulcan circling the Sun within Mercury's orbit, cannot be squared with the finding that the value predicted by general relativity agreed with the observed residual without invoking any additional matter, since a relativistic account that needs no extra mass leaves no gravitational work for such a planet to do.

data.question: How did researchers resolve the dispute over whether mitochondria arose from an endosymbiotic bacterium or from the invagination of a host cell membrane?

  4. The autogenous hypothesis held that mitochondria formed by the infolding of the host cell's own membranes. TRUE
  5. Margit Nass and Sylvan Nass reported DNA inside mitochondria in 1963 using electron microscopy. TRUE

  7. Mitochondria contain no DNA of their own. TRUE
  8. Mitochondrial ribosomes are inhibited by the antibacterial antibiotic chloramphenicol. TRUE
  9. The mitochondrial inner membrane contains cardiolipin, a lipid characteristic of bacterial membranes. TRUE
  10. Carl Woese established small-subunit ribosomal RNA sequence comparison as a method for reconstructing deep phylogeny. TRUE
  11. Ribosomal RNA phylogenies placed the mitochondrial lineage inside the alphaproteobacteria. TRUE
  12. Phylogenetic analyses of mitochondrial genes place the organelle within the cyanobacteria. FALSE

[1] after “The decisive evidence came from the comparison of sequences rather than of structures.”

The placement of the mitochondrial lineage inside the alphaproteobacteria by ribosomal RNA phylogenies was brought about by Carl Woese's establishment of small-subunit ribosomal RNA sequence comparison as a method for reconstructing deep phylogeny.
data.b_html:
[1] after “The decisive evidence came from the comparison of sequences rather than of structures.”

Carl Woese established small-subunit ribosomal RNA sequence comparison as a method for reconstructing deep phylogeny, and that methodological advance led directly to the placement of the mitochondrial lineage inside the alphaproteobacteria by ribosomal RNA phylogenies.
data.context_html:
Show the rest of the response (the same in A and B; [k] marks where they differ)

The question was contested from the moment the modern endosymbiotic proposal appeared in print. Lynn Margulis published the paper "On the Origin of Mitosing Cells" in 1967, at a time when the ultrastructure of eukaryotic organelles was far better characterized than their ancestry. Margulis argued that mitochondria descended from free-living aerobic bacteria taken up by a host cell, and that argument cannot be squared with the proposal, set out in Margulis's 1967 paper, that mitochondria arose by invagination of the host plasma membrane; one origin excludes the other, so the two cannot both hold of the same organelle. By contrast, the autogenous hypothesis held that mitochondria formed by the infolding of the host cell's own membranes.

Resolving the matter required characters that a mere infolding of host membrane could not plausibly carry. Margit Nass and Sylvan Nass reported DNA inside mitochondria in 1963 using electron microscopy, and their micrographs show that mitochondria retain a genome of their own that is distinct from the nuclear genome. On this point the possibilities are strict and mutually exclusive: either mitochondria retain such a separate genome of their own, or mitochondria contain no DNA of their own, and exactly one of these two situations can obtain.

A further line of work addressed the biochemistry of the organelle rather than its appearance in section, using the tools of pharmacology and lipid analysis. At least one of the following is the case, and quite possibly both at once: mitochondrial ribosomes are inhibited by the antibacterial antibiotic chloramphenicol, and the mitochondrial inner membrane contains cardiolipin, a lipid characteristic of bacterial membranes.

The decisive evidence came from the comparison of sequences rather than of structures. [1] A ribosomal placement among the alphaproteobacteria and a placement among the cyanobacteria cannot both be true of one and the same organelle, and phylogenetic analyses of mitochondrial genes place the organelle within the cyanobacteria. The alphaproteobacterial affiliation indicates that mitochondria arose from a free-living bacterium that was engulfed by an ancestral host cell; in other words, the mitochondrial lineage descends from a prokaryotic symbiont that was taken up by an ancestral cell.

The manner in which the controversy closed is instructive about method in evolutionary cell biology. Ultrastructural appearance alone could not discriminate between the competing accounts of organelle origin, since an infolded membrane compartment and an engulfed cell may look much alike in thin section, and arguments from morphology were accordingly inconclusive for decades. What discriminated in the end was heritable information: nucleic acid read as sequence and interpreted as a branching genealogy. Once comparative sequence analysis supplied a determinate branching order with identifiable prokaryotic relatives, the question ceased to be a matter of competing interpretations of images and became one admitting a testable answer.
